about: Materials 1 (AERO40005) is a 5-credit core module in the first year (Autumn term) of Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering (H401). It connects the microstructure of materials to their mechanical behaviour and introduces materials selection and fracture. The department's module page lists Materials 1 as Year 1 core but its detailed descriptor could not be opened, so the nine topics here (from stress–strain behaviour and selection, through elasticity, bonding, dislocations and strengthening, to yield criteria, fracture and the material classes) follow a topic summary recorded from the department's module information that could not be re-verified against the descriptor; treat the order and coverage as a guide. The department's 2026–27 coursework schedule lists a lab data analysis assignment due after each laboratory session; weightings were not confirmed, so check the current descriptor.

notes.h: The tensile test and the stress–strain curve
notes.body:
Almost every mechanical property used in aircraft design comes from a simple experiment: pull a specimen in tension and record load against extension. Learning to read the resulting curve underpins almost everything else in materials for structures.

Engineering stress and strain
- Engineering stress σ = F/A0, where A0 is the original cross-sectional area (units Pa; MPa = N/mm²).
- Engineering strain ε = ΔL/L0 (dimensionless).
- Example: an aluminium alloy rod of diameter 10 mm carries 15 kN. A0 = π(0.010)²/4 = 7.85 × 10⁻⁵ m², so σ = 191 MPa. With E ≈ 70 GPa the strain is 191/70,000 = 2.73 × 10⁻³, so a 2 m rod extends by about 5.5 mm.

Features of the curve (ductile metal)
- Linear elastic region: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus. Unloading returns along the same line.
- Yield: the onset of permanent (plastic) deformation. Where there is no sharp yield point, the 0.2% proof stress is used: draw a line parallel to the elastic slope starting at ε = 0.002 and read where it meets the curve.
- Work hardening: beyond yield the stress needed keeps rising as the material deforms.
- Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the maximum engineering stress. After it the specimen necks (deformation concentrates locally) and the engineering stress falls until fracture.
- Ductility: the plastic strain at fracture, quoted as % elongation, or as % reduction in area.
- Unloading from the plastic region follows a line of slope E, leaving a permanent strain.

True stress and true strain
- True stress σt = F/A uses the current area. True strain εt = ∫dL/L = ln(L/L0) = ln(1 + ε).
- Plastic deformation is close to constant volume, so before necking σt = σ(1 + ε). At ε = 0.2, εt = ln 1.2 = 0.182.
- Necking begins when the rate of work hardening can no longer keep up with the loss of area: the Considère condition dσt/dεt = σt. Considère's construction shows this graphically: on a plot of true stress against engineering strain, draw a tangent to the curve from the point ε = −1 on the strain axis; the point where it touches the curve is where necking starts (the UTS).

Energy
- Elastic energy stored per unit volume = ½σε = σ²/2E. At 191 MPa in the aluminium above this is about 0.26 MJ/m³.
- The area under the whole curve is the energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture, a rough indicator of how much damage a material can absorb.

Poisson's ratio
- Under uniaxial tension the specimen narrows: ν = −(lateral strain)/(axial strain). Approximately 0.3 for most metals, close to 0.5 for rubber.

Different classes give very different curves. Ceramics and glasses are linear up to brittle fracture with almost no plasticity; polymers can show yielding, cold drawing and strong dependence on strain rate and temperature.

Exam tips: convert diameters to areas carefully (area uses d²/4), keep units consistent (MPa with mm² and N), and say which strain you mean (engineering or true).

notes.h: Materials selection: performance indices and property charts
notes.body:
Choosing a material is a design decision, and in aerospace the usual goal is minimum mass for a required stiffness or strength. The systematic method (developed by Ashby) combines the design requirements into a performance index and then uses property charts to rank materials.

The method
- Function: what does the component do (tie, beam, panel, pressure vessel)?
- Objective: what is minimised or maximised (mass, cost, energy)?
- Constraints: what must be met (stiffness, strength, temperature, corrosion)?
- Free variables: what can the designer change (usually the cross-section and the material)?
Write the objective as an equation, eliminate the free variable using the constraint, and what remains splits into a function of the material properties: the index.

Light stiff tie (length L, axial stiffness S)
- Stiffness S = EA/L, so A = SL/E.
- Mass m = ALρ = SL²(ρ/E).
- Minimise mass by maximising E/ρ (the specific stiffness).
With approximate handbook values, steel (E ≈ 210 GPa, ρ ≈ 7.8 Mg/m³), aluminium (≈ 70 GPa, 2.7 Mg/m³) and titanium (≈ 115 GPa, 4.5 Mg/m³) all have E/ρ close to 26 GPa/(Mg/m³), which is why no common metal beats another for a stiff tie.

Light stiff beam (square section of side b, fixed L, bending stiffness S)
- S = C·EI/L³ with I = b⁴/12, so b² = (12SL³/CE)^(1/2).
- m = b²Lρ ∝ ρ/E^(1/2), so maximise E^(1/2)/ρ.
- Aluminium: √70/2.7 ≈ 3.1; steel: √210/7.8 ≈ 1.9. An aluminium beam of equal stiffness weighs about 0.60 of the steel one.

Light stiff panel (fixed width and length, thickness free)
- I = wt³/12, so t ∝ E^(−1/3) and the index is E^(1/3)/ρ. The lower the exponent on E, the more low-density materials (wood, foams, CFRP) win.

Strength-limited designs
- Light strong tie: σf/ρ.
- Light strong beam: σf^(2/3)/ρ.
- Light strong panel: σf^(1/2)/ρ.

Property charts
- Plot E against ρ (or σf against ρ) on log scales. Each material class forms a bubble.
- An index M = E^(1/n)/ρ is constant along a line log E = n·log ρ + n·log M, so lines of slope 1 (ties), 2 (beams) and 3 (panels) are guidelines. Moving the line towards the top left selects better materials.
- Illustrative approximate values for a beam: spruce along the grain (E ≈ 10 GPa, ρ ≈ 0.45 Mg/m³) gives √E/ρ ≈ 7, and a CFRP with E ≈ 100 GPa, ρ ≈ 1.6 Mg/m³ gives ≈ 6, far above the metals. This is why composites and, historically, wood are so attractive in light structures.

Beyond the index
Real choices also need screening by temperature, toughness, fatigue, environment, manufacturability and cost. The index ranks; engineering judgement decides.

Exam tips: always write the objective, constraint and free variable before deriving an index, and state the slope of the guideline on a log–log chart.

notes.h: Elasticity in three dimensions and the types of atomic bond
notes.body:
Real components carry stresses in more than one direction, so the one-dimensional law σ = Eε has to be generalised. At the same time, the elastic constants themselves come from the bonds between atoms, which also explain why the material classes behave so differently.

Generalised Hooke's law (isotropic material)
- εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E, and similarly for εy and εz by cycling the subscripts.
- Shear: γ = τ/G.
- The three constants are linked: G = E/[2(1 + ν)] and the bulk modulus K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)].
- For steel with E ≈ 200 GPa and ν = 0.3: G ≈ 76.9 GPa, K ≈ 167 GPa.
- Volumetric strain ΔV/V = εx + εy + εz = (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E. For ν = 0.5 this is zero: the material is incompressible (rubber is close to this).

Worked example: an aluminium alloy plate (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33) has σx = 100 MPa, σy = 50 MPa, σz = 0.
- εx = (100 − 0.33 × 50)/70,000 = 1.19 × 10⁻³.
- εy = (50 − 0.33 × 100)/70,000 = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.
- εz = −0.33 × 150/70,000 = −7.1 × 10⁻⁴: the plate gets thinner although there is no stress through the thickness.

Note that a constrained material can be stiffer than E suggests: if lateral strains are prevented (a thin layer between rigid plates, say), Poisson effects build up lateral stresses.

Atomic bonding
Primary (strong) bonds:
- Ionic: electrons transferred, ions held by electrostatic attraction; non-directional (e.g. NaCl, many ceramic oxides). Brittle because like ions repel when planes slide.
- Covalent: electrons shared; strongly directional (diamond, silicon, the carbon backbone of polymers, many ceramics such as SiC). High stiffness and melting point.
- Metallic: positive ions in a "sea" of delocalised electrons; non-directional, allowing atoms to slide past each other, which is why metals can be ductile and conduct electricity.
Secondary (weak) bonds:
- Van der Waals: weak attraction between fluctuating dipoles.
- Hydrogen bonds: between hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom and a neighbouring electronegative atom (water, nylon).

Linking bonds to classes
- Metals: metallic bonds, crystalline packing (FCC, BCC, HCP).
- Ceramics and glasses: ionic and covalent bonds; crystalline or amorphous (glass).
- Polymers: covalent bonds along chains, but secondary bonds between chains, which control their low stiffness below the glass transition.
- Composites combine classes, e.g. carbon fibres (covalent) in an epoxy matrix.

Bond energy relates to melting point: strong primary bonds give high melting points, secondary bonds low ones.

Exam tips: write the three generalised Hooke equations out in full before substituting, keep signs consistent (tension positive), and quote the G–E–ν and K–E–ν relations exactly.

Why is steel about a hundred times stiffer than nylon, and rubber a thousand times less stiff again? The answer lies in the stiffness of the bonds between atoms and how they are arranged.

The interatomic force law
- Two atoms attract at long range and repel strongly at short range. The net force F(r) is zero at the equilibrium spacing r0, where the potential energy U(r) has its minimum (F = dU/dr).
- For small displacements, each bond behaves like a spring of stiffness S0 = (dF/dr) at r = r0 = (d²U/dr²) at r0.
- Stress on a plane of atoms is roughly the force per bond divided by the area per bond, about r0², and strain is the displacement divided by r0. So E ≈ S0/r0.

Orders of magnitude (approximate)
- Primary bonds (covalent, ionic, metallic) have S0 of roughly 10–200 N/m. With r0 of about 0.2–0.3 nm this gives E from tens to hundreds of GPa, matching metals and ceramics. Example: S0 = 50 N/m, r0 = 0.2 nm gives E ≈ 50/(0.2 × 10⁻⁹) = 250 GPa.
- Secondary bonds (van der Waals and hydrogen bonds) have S0 of roughly 0.5–2 N/m, giving E of a few GPa, the right order for glassy polymers.
- The method is approximate (it ignores the detailed geometry of the crystal), but it explains the ranking of material classes.

Polymers and the glass transition
- Below the glass transition temperature Tg, secondary bonds between chains are intact and the polymer is glassy (E of a few GPa).
- Above Tg the secondary bonds have effectively melted. If the chains are lightly cross-linked, the material is a rubber whose stiffness comes from entropy (chains being uncoiled), and E falls to a few MPa.
- Cross-link density increases the rubbery modulus, so a heavily cross-linked thermoset such as an epoxy keeps a higher modulus above Tg than a lightly cross-linked rubber, although it still softens markedly.

Density
- Density depends on atomic mass and how closely atoms pack. Metals (heavy atoms, close-packed structures) are dense; polymers (light C and H atoms, loose packing) are light. The spread of density across engineering materials is much smaller than the spread of modulus, which is why modulus dominates many selection decisions.

Composites: bounds on modulus
For aligned fibres with volume fraction Vf:
- Along the fibres (equal strain, Voigt): E∥ = VfEf + (1 − Vf)Em.
- Across the fibres (equal stress, Reuss): 1/E⊥ = Vf/Ef + (1 − Vf)/Em.
- Example: carbon fibre (Ef ≈ 230 GPa) in epoxy (Em ≈ 3 GPa), Vf = 0.6: E∥ ≈ 139 GPa but E⊥ ≈ 7.4 GPa. The huge anisotropy is why aerospace laminates stack plies at several angles (0°, ±45°, 90°).

Temperature
Modulus falls slowly with temperature in metals and ceramics, and dramatically near Tg in polymers, which limits the service temperature of polymer-matrix composites.

Exam tips: convert nanometres to metres before dividing (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m), check that your answer falls in the expected range for the material class, and state which rule of mixtures (equal strain or equal stress) you are using.

notes.h: Yield, ductility and the role of dislocations
notes.body:
A perfect crystal should be enormously strong. Real metals yield at stresses hundreds to thousands of times lower. The explanation, and the key to controlling strength, is the dislocation.

Ideal strength
- To slide one plane of atoms over another in a perfect crystal, every bond across the plane must be stretched at once.
- A simple sinusoidal model (Frenkel) gives an ideal shear strength of about G/2π; more realistic force laws give lower values, of order G/30. Either way this is several GPa for metals.
- Measured shear yield stresses of pure, annealed metals are much smaller, often by factors of a hundred to many thousands.

Dislocations
- A dislocation is a line defect in a crystal. Slip happens by moving the dislocation across the slip plane, breaking and remaking bonds one line at a time rather than all at once, which needs a much smaller stress (like moving a ruck along a carpet).
- Burgers vector b: the closure failure of a circuit drawn round the dislocation; its size is about one atomic spacing (e.g. about 0.25–0.29 nm in common metals).
- Edge dislocation: b perpendicular to the line (an extra half-plane of atoms). Screw dislocation: b parallel to the line. Mixed dislocations have b at another angle.
- When a dislocation sweeps across the whole slip plane the crystal is offset by b.

Forces on dislocations
- A shear stress τ on the slip plane exerts a force f = τb per unit length on the dislocation. Example: τ = 40 MPa and b = 0.25 nm give f = 0.01 N/m.
- Dislocations have a line tension T ≈ Gb²/2: they behave like stretched elastic strings, which matters for strengthening by obstacles.
- The resistance of the lattice itself (lattice friction) is low in close-packed metals but very high in ceramics with directional covalent or ionic bonds.

From single crystals to polycrystals
- Slip happens on particular planes and directions (slip systems). FCC metals (aluminium, copper, nickel) have many slip systems and stay ductile even at low temperature.
- In a polycrystal each grain must deform compatibly with its neighbours, so the tensile yield strength is roughly three times the shear yield strength of a crystal: σy ≈ 3τy.

Ductility
- Ductile materials deform plastically before fracture (large elongation, necking, dimpled fracture surfaces). They give warning and absorb energy.
- Brittle materials fracture with little plastic strain. Ceramics are brittle because dislocations hardly move in them at room temperature.
- Some BCC metals, including ordinary carbon steels, show a ductile-to-brittle transition as temperature falls; FCC metals do not.

Why this matters to aerospace engineers
Aluminium alloys (FCC) keep their toughness at the low temperatures met at altitude. Controlling dislocation motion, rather than eliminating dislocations, is how alloys are made strong while remaining ductile enough to tolerate damage.

Exam tips: be precise about the geometry of edge and screw dislocations, quote f = τb with units (N/m), and explain clearly why the real yield strength is so far below the ideal.

notes.h: Plastic flow and how alloys are strengthened
notes.body:
Since plastic flow is the movement of dislocations, a metal is made stronger by making dislocations harder to move. Each strengthening mechanism puts different obstacles in their way. Aerospace alloys use several mechanisms at once.

Solid solution strengthening
- Dissolved atoms of a different size (substitutional, e.g. Mg in Al, or interstitial, e.g. C in Fe) distort the lattice locally. The resulting strain fields interact with dislocations and resist their motion.
- Strength rises with solute concentration.

Precipitation (age) hardening
- Fine, closely spaced particles of a second phase block dislocations. A dislocation must bow between particles of spacing L.
- Force balance: the force on the bowed segment τbL is balanced by the line tension at both ends, 2T, so τ = 2T/(bL). With T ≈ Gb²/2 this gives τ ≈ Gb/L (the Orowan stress).
- Example: aluminium (G ≈ 26 GPa, b ≈ 0.286 nm) with precipitates 100 nm apart: τ ≈ 26 × 10⁹ × 0.286 × 10⁻⁹/(100 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 74 MPa, so σy ≈ 3τ ≈ 220 MPa. Halving the spacing doubles the strengthening.
- Heat treatment of age-hardenable Al alloys (such as the 2xxx Al–Cu and 7xxx Al–Zn–Mg–Cu families used in airframes):
 - solution treat at high temperature (around 500 °C, depending on the alloy) to dissolve the alloying elements;
 - quench to trap them in a supersaturated solid solution;
 - age (at room temperature or a moderately raised temperature) so that fine precipitates form.
- Over-ageing (too long or too hot) lets precipitates coarsen; their spacing grows and strength falls.

Work (strain) hardening
- Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations; they tangle and obstruct each other, so the flow stress rises with strain. Cold rolling or drawing uses this.
- Annealing (heating) lets dislocations rearrange and new grains form, restoring ductility and lowering strength.

Grain-boundary strengthening
- Grain boundaries block slip because neighbouring grains have different orientations. Finer grains mean more boundaries.
- Hall–Petch relation: σy = σ0 + k·d^(−1/2), where d is grain size. Reducing d by a factor of 4 doubles the grain-boundary term. Example with given constants σ0 = 70 MPa and k = 0.74 MPa m^(1/2): d = 25 µm gives d^(−1/2) = 200 m^(−1/2) and σy = 70 + 148 = 218 MPa.
- Fine grains are unusual in raising both strength and toughness.

The dislocation yield strength
Contributions are often roughly added: σy ≈ σ(lattice) + σ(solution) + σ(precipitates) + σ(work hardening) + σ(grain boundaries).

Trade-offs
- Strengthening usually costs ductility and sometimes toughness.
- Heat from welding or service can undo precipitation hardening or work hardening, which is one reason many aluminium airframes are riveted rather than welded.

Exam tips: derive the Orowan stress from the force balance rather than quoting it, remember the factor of about 3 between τy and σy, and be clear about the purpose of each heat-treatment step.

notes.h: Yield under combined stresses and the basics of fracture
notes.body:
A tensile test gives the yield strength σy under uniaxial stress. Aircraft structures, such as a pressurised fuselage, a wing skin or a shaft under torsion, carry combined stresses. Yield criteria predict when yielding starts in these cases using only σy.

Principal stresses
- Any stress state can be described by three principal stresses σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3 acting on planes with no shear.
- In plane stress with σx, σy and τxy: σ1,2 = (σx + σy)/2 ± √{[(σx − σy)/2]² + τxy²}, with the third principal stress zero.
- Yielding in metals depends on shear (dislocation glide) and is essentially unaffected by hydrostatic pressure, so the criteria use differences of principal stresses.

Tresca (maximum shear stress) criterion
- Yield occurs when the maximum shear stress (σ1 − σ3)/2 reaches σy/2, i.e. σ1 − σ3 = σy.
- In pure shear (σ1 = τ, σ3 = −τ) this gives τy = σy/2.

Von Mises (distortion energy) criterion
- Yield occurs when (σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)² = 2σy².
- Equivalently the von Mises stress σvm = √{½[(σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)²]} reaches σy.
- In pure shear τy = σy/√3 ≈ 0.577σy. Experiments on ductile metals usually lie closer to von Mises; Tresca is slightly conservative and simpler.
- For direct stress σ plus shear τ (a shaft under tension and torsion): σvm = √(σ² + 3τ²), and the Tresca equivalent is √(σ² + 4τ²).

Worked example: a pressurised fuselage
- A thin-walled cylinder of radius r and wall thickness t with pressure difference p has hoop stress σθ = pr/t and axial stress σz = pr/2t; the radial stress is small (≈ 0).
- With r = 2 m, t = 2 mm, p = 60 kPa: σθ = 60 MPa, σz = 30 MPa, σr ≈ 0.
- Tresca: σ1 − σ3 = 60 − 0 = 60 MPa. Von Mises: √{½[(60 − 30)² + 30² + 60²]} = 52.0 MPa. Both are well below the yield strength of an aluminium alloy, but this ignores stress concentrations at windows and joints.

Fracture basics
- Ductile fracture: extensive plastic flow, necking, then voids nucleate at particles, grow and coalesce, leaving a dimpled surface.
- Brittle fracture: a crack runs with little plasticity, often by cleavage along crystal planes, leaving a flat, shiny surface.
- Holes, notches and cracks concentrate stress. For an elliptical hole of half-length a and tip radius ρ in a wide plate, the peak stress is σmax = σ(1 + 2√(a/ρ)); a circular hole (a = ρ) gives a factor of 3. For a sharp crack ρ is tiny and the elastic peak stress becomes very large, which is why fracture mechanics (next topic) is needed.
- In ductile materials local yielding blunts the crack tip and redistributes the stress; in brittle ones it does not.

Exam tips: order the principal stresses before applying Tresca, include the zero principal stress in plane-stress problems, and quote both criteria for pure shear.

notes.h: Fast fracture, stress intensity and toughness
notes.body:
Aircraft structures must be designed on the assumption that cracks exist, from manufacture, corrosion or fatigue. Fracture mechanics answers the question: at what stress will a crack of a given size suddenly run? The de Havilland Comet losses of 1954, traced to fatigue cracks growing from corners of fuselage openings under repeated pressurisation, are the classic reminder of why this matters.

Energy view (Griffith)
- A growing crack releases stored elastic energy but must supply energy to create new surfaces (and, in metals, to do plastic work at the tip).
- Fast fracture occurs when the energy released per unit area of crack growth, G, reaches the material's toughness Gc (units J/m²).
- For a through-crack of length 2a in a large plate under remote stress σ, fast fracture occurs when σ√(πa) = √(EGc).

Stress intensity factor
- The crack-tip stress field scales with K = Yσ√(πa), units MPa√m. Y is a geometry factor (≈ 1 for a central through-crack of length 2a in a wide plate; about 1.12 for an edge crack).
- Fast fracture when K = Kc, the fracture toughness, a material property.
- Kc and Gc are linked: Kc² = EGc (plane stress; a factor (1 − ν²) appears in plane strain). For Kc = 30 MPa√m and E = 70 GPa, Gc = (30 × 10⁶)²/(70 × 10⁹) ≈ 12.9 kJ/m².

Worked example
A wide aluminium alloy panel (Kc ≈ 30 MPa√m, an approximate value) carries 200 MPa.
- A central crack of total length 10 mm (a = 5 mm) gives K = 200√(π × 0.005) = 25.1 MPa√m, below Kc: safe.
- Critical half-length: ac = (Kc/σ)²/π = (30/200)²/π = 7.2 mm, i.e. a total crack length of about 14.3 mm.
- Because ac ∝ 1/σ², doubling the stress cuts the critical crack size to a quarter.

Typical (approximate) fracture toughness values
- Window glass: under 1 MPa√m.
- Engineering ceramics such as alumina: a few MPa√m.
- Epoxy resins: roughly 0.5–2 MPa√m.
- Aluminium alloys: a few tens of MPa√m.
- Tough steels and titanium alloys: up to around 100 MPa√m or more.
Toughness and strength often trade off: heat treatments that raise strength frequently lower Kc.

Design ideas
- Yield before fracture: a component with a crack of length a yields before it fractures if a < Kc²/(πσy²). Materials with high Kc/σy tolerate larger cracks.
- Damage tolerance: aircraft are inspected at intervals chosen so that any crack is found before it reaches ac. Larger ac (tougher material, lower stress) gives longer inspection intervals.
- Leak before break: in a pressure vessel, the crack should be able to grow through the wall (and leak, detectably) before it reaches the critical length.
- Thickness matters: thick sections constrain the crack tip (plane strain) and show lower measured toughness than thin sheets.

Exam tips: always state whether a is the half-length or the full crack length, convert mm to m inside the square root, and quote K in MPa√m.

notes.h: Metals, polymers, ceramics and composites in aerospace
notes.body:
This topic surveys the material classes, linking their bonding and microstructure to the properties that matter in aircraft and spacecraft. The values given are approximate and vary widely within each class.

Metals
- Metallic bonding, crystalline (FCC, BCC, HCP). High modulus (about 45 GPa for magnesium up to about 200 GPa for steels), ductile, tough, good in fatigue when well designed, electrically and thermally conducting.
- Aluminium alloys (ρ ≈ 2.7 Mg/m³, E ≈ 70 GPa): the traditional airframe material, strengthened by precipitation (2xxx, 7xxx series). Lose much of their strength at moderate temperatures, and can corrode.
- Titanium alloys (ρ ≈ 4.5 Mg/m³, E ≈ 110–120 GPa): high strength-to-weight ratio, good corrosion resistance and higher service temperature than aluminium; used in highly loaded structure, engine fans and compressors, and next to carbon composites because aluminium in contact with carbon fibre suffers galvanic corrosion.
- Steels (ρ ≈ 7.8 Mg/m³, E ≈ 210 GPa): very high strength, used where size is limited, e.g. landing gear.
- Nickel-based superalloys: retain strength and creep resistance at the very high temperatures in turbine sections.

Polymers
- Covalent chains with secondary bonds between them. Low density (about 0.9–1.5 Mg/m³), low modulus (a few GPa for glassy polymers).
- Thermoplastics (linear or branched chains) soften on heating and can be remelted. Thermosets (heavily cross-linked, e.g. epoxy) do not melt and are the usual matrix of aerospace composites. Elastomers are lightly cross-linked and used above Tg (seals, tyres).
- Properties depend strongly on temperature relative to Tg and on loading rate (viscoelasticity). Many polymers creep noticeably at room temperature.

Ceramics and glasses
- Ionic and covalent bonds. High modulus, very hard, high melting points, good chemical stability, low density compared with steel.
- Brittle: low fracture toughness, so strength is controlled by the largest flaw. Strength in compression is far higher than in tension (often around ten times or more).
- Uses: thermal barrier coatings on turbine blades, heat shields, bearings, radomes.

Statistics of brittle strength: Weibull
- Because the critical flaw varies from sample to sample, strength is a distribution. The survival probability under stress σ is Ps = exp[−(σ/σ0)^m], where m is the Weibull modulus and σ0 a reference stress.
- High m means consistent strength (metals behave as if m were very large); ceramics typically have m of roughly 5–20.
- Example: m = 10, σ0 = 300 MPa, σ = 200 MPa: Ps = exp[−(2/3)^10] = 0.983, so about 1.7% of samples fail.
- Larger components contain more flaws: Ps(V) = exp[−(V/V0)(σ/σ0)^m]. Ten times the volume at the same stress gives Ps = exp(−10 × 0.0173) = 0.84.

Composites
- Combine stiff, strong fibres (carbon, glass, aramid) with a tough matrix (usually epoxy). Very high specific stiffness and strength along the fibres, but anisotropic, sensitive to impact damage and delamination, and limited in temperature by the matrix.
- Composites now make up about half the structural weight of the latest wide-body airliners (e.g. the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350).

Exam tips: link each property back to bonding and microstructure, quote approximate values with "about", and be ready to justify a material choice for a named aircraft component.

cards.b: The stress where a line parallel to the elastic slope, offset to 0.2% strain, meets the curve; used as the yield strength when there is no sharp yield point.

cards.f: True strain in terms of engineering strain

cards.b: σt = σ(1 + ε), assuming constant volume during plastic deformation.
Necking starts when dσt/dεt = σt, i.e. work hardening can no longer compensate for the falling cross-section.

cards.f: Elastic strain energy per unit volume
cards.b: σ²/(2E), the area under the linear-elastic part of the curve (½σε).
The maximum engineering stress in a tensile test; necking begins there in a ductile metal.
ν = −lateral strain/axial strain under uniaxial load; about 0.3 for metals and close to 0.5 for rubber.

cards.f: Index for a light, stiff tie
cards.b: Maximise E/ρ (from m = SL²ρ/E).

cards.f: Index for a light, stiff beam
cards.b: Maximise E^(1/2)/ρ (square section scaled with fixed length).

cards.f: Index for a light, stiff panel
cards.b: Maximise E^(1/3)/ρ (thickness is the free variable).

cards.f: Index for a light, strong beam
cards.b: Maximise σf^(2/3)/ρ.

cards.f: Slope of guideline for E^(1/2)/ρ on a log E vs log ρ chart
cards.b: 2 (log E = 2 log ρ + constant).

cards.f: Why do steel, aluminium and titanium perform similarly as stiff ties?
cards.b: Their specific stiffness E/ρ is about the same, roughly 25–27 GPa/(Mg/m³) using approximate handbook values.

cards.f: Free variable in a selection problem
cards.b: A design parameter the designer may change (often the cross-section) that is eliminated using the constraint to leave a material index.
εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E for an isotropic linear-elastic material.

cards.f: Relation between G, E and ν
Bulk modulus in terms of E and ν
cards.b: K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]; it becomes infinite as ν → 0.5 (incompressible).
ΔV/V = εx + εy + εz = (1 − 2ν)(σx + σy + σz)/E.
Ionic (electron transfer, non-directional), covalent (shared electrons, directional), metallic (delocalised electrons, non-directional).
Van der Waals (fluctuating dipoles) and hydrogen bonds; much weaker than primary bonds.

cards.f: Why is a polymer's stiffness low below Tg despite covalent chains?
cards.b: Deformation mainly stretches the weak secondary bonds between chains, not the covalent bonds along them.
The slope of the interatomic force–separation curve at the equilibrium spacing: S0 = (dF/dr) at r0 = (d²U/dr²) at r0.

cards.f: Estimate of E from bond stiffness
cards.b: E ≈ S0/r0. For S0 = 50 N/m and r0 = 0.2 nm, E ≈ 250 GPa.
Temperature above which secondary bonds between polymer chains melt; modulus drops from a few GPa (glassy) to a few MPa (rubbery, if cross-linked).
E∥ = VfEf + (1 − Vf)Em (equal strain, upper bound).
1/E⊥ = Vf/Ef + (1 − Vf)/Em (equal stress, lower bound).

cards.f: Why do CFRP laminates use plies at several angles?
cards.b: A unidirectional ply is very stiff along the fibres but weak and compliant across them (e.g. about 139 vs 7 GPa), so plies are stacked at 0°, ±45°, 90° to carry loads in all directions.
Entropy: stretching uncoils the cross-linked chains into less probable configurations, and they tend to recoil.
The closure failure of a circuit around a dislocation: the magnitude and direction of the lattice offset it produces; about one atomic spacing.
Edge: Burgers vector perpendicular to the dislocation line (extra half-plane). Screw: Burgers vector parallel to the line.

cards.f: Force per unit length on a dislocation
cards.b: f = τb, where τ is the shear stress on the slip plane. E.g. 40 MPa × 0.25 nm = 0.01 N/m.
T ≈ Gb²/2: energy per unit length, acting like the tension in a string.

cards.f: Why real yield strengths are far below ideal
cards.b: Dislocations allow slip by breaking bonds one line at a time rather than across a whole plane simultaneously.

cards.f: Polycrystal yield strength vs crystal shear yield stress
cards.b: σy ≈ 3τy, reflecting the need for many slip systems to operate in randomly oriented grains.

cards.f: Why ceramics are brittle at room temperature
cards.b: Their directional covalent/ionic bonds give a very high lattice resistance, so dislocations barely move and cracks propagate first.
τ ≈ Gb/L, from the force balance τbL = 2T with line tension T ≈ Gb²/2; L is the obstacle spacing.
σy = σ0 + k·d^(−1/2): yield strength rises as grain size d falls.
Solution treat (dissolve solute), quench (supersaturated solid solution), age (fine precipitates form).
Ageing too long or too hot lets precipitates coarsen; their spacing increases and strength falls (τ ≈ Gb/L).
Plastic strain multiplies dislocations, which tangle and block one another, raising the flow stress.
Solute atoms of different size distort the lattice; their strain fields impede dislocation motion.

cards.f: Effect of annealing a cold-worked metal
cards.b: Dislocations recover and new strain-free grains recrystallise: strength falls, ductility returns.
Yield when the maximum shear stress reaches σy/2: σ1 − σ3 = σy.
Yield when (σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)² = 2σy².

cards.f: Shear yield stress by Tresca and von Mises
cards.b: Tresca: τy = σy/2 = 0.5σy. Von Mises: τy = σy/√3 ≈ 0.577σy.
Hoop σθ = pr/t; axial σz = pr/(2t); radial stress ≈ 0 for thin walls.

cards.f: Equivalent stresses for σ plus τ
cards.b: Von Mises: √(σ² + 3τ²); Tresca: √(σ² + 4τ²).

cards.f: Stress concentration at an elliptical hole
cards.b: σmax = σ(1 + 2√(a/ρ)); a circular hole gives a factor of 3.

cards.f: Why does hydrostatic pressure not appear in yield criteria for metals?
cards.b: Yield is by dislocation glide driven by shear; a hydrostatic stress adds no shear, so only principal stress differences matter.
K = Yσ√(πa); Y is a geometry factor (≈ 1 for a central crack of length 2a in a wide plate). Units MPa√m.
K = Kc, where Kc is the fracture toughness of the material.
Kc² = EGc (plane stress). For Kc = 30 MPa√m, E = 70 GPa: Gc ≈ 12.9 kJ/m².
ac = (Kc/Yσ)²/π. It scales as 1/σ², so doubling stress quarters the critical crack.
a < Kc²/(πσy²): materials with high Kc/σy tolerate larger cracks before fast fracture.
Design principle that a crack in a pressure vessel should penetrate the wall and leak detectably before reaching the critical size for fast fracture.

cards.f: Approximate Kc of aluminium alloys vs glass
cards.b: Aluminium alloys: a few tens of MPa√m. Glass: below 1 MPa√m (approximate values).
Ps = exp[−(σ/σ0)^m]; m is the Weibull modulus. Higher m means less scatter in strength.

cards.f: Effect of volume on brittle strength
cards.b: Ps(V) = exp[−(V/V0)(σ/σ0)^m]: larger components contain more flaws, so they are more likely to fail at a given stress.
Thermoplastics have uncrosslinked chains and soften/melt on heating; thermosets are heavily cross-linked, do not melt, and decompose instead.

cards.f: Why titanium is used next to CFRP in airframes
cards.b: Aluminium in contact with carbon fibre suffers galvanic corrosion; titanium is far more compatible and also has high specific strength.

cards.f: Why ceramics are much stronger in compression than tension
cards.b: In tension a flaw opens and propagates by fast fracture; in compression flaws are closed and failure needs widespread crushing, so compressive strength is often around ten times higher.
Alloys that keep strength and creep resistance at very high temperatures; used in the hot turbine sections of jet engines.

cards.f: Approximate density and modulus of aluminium vs titanium alloys
cards.b: Al: about 2.7 Mg/m³ and 70 GPa. Ti: about 4.5 Mg/m³ and 110–120 GPa.

questions.q: A rod of diameter 10 mm carries an axial load of 15 kN. What is the axial stress?
questions.why: A = πd²/4 = π × 10²/4 = 78.5 mm², so σ = 15,000/78.5 = 191 MPa. 47.7 MPa comes from using the diameter as if it were the radius (A = π × 10² = 314 mm²). 150 MPa comes from using d² = 100 mm² as the area, i.e. treating the section as a 10 mm square. 600 MPa comes from using r² = 25 mm² as the area, leaving out the π.

questions.q: A specimen is stretched uniformly to an engineering strain of 0.20. What is the true strain?
questions.why: True strain is ln(1 + ε) = ln 1.2 = 0.182. 0.200 simply repeats the engineering strain, which overestimates the true strain at large deformations. 0.240 multiplies the strain by (1 + ε), the factor used to convert engineering stress to true stress, not strain. 0.167 is ε/(1 + ε), the change in length divided by the final length instead of integrating dL/L.

questions.q: A metal specimen with a 50 mm gauge length is stretched uniformly to 60 mm while the engineering stress is 400 MPa. Find the engineering strain, true strain and true stress, stating the assumption used.
markScheme: Engineering strain = 10/50 = 0.20
True strain = ln(60/50) = 0.182
True stress = σ(1 + ε) = 400 × 1.2 = 480 MPa
Assumes constant volume (plastic flow) and uniform deformation (no necking yet)
questions.modelAnswer: Engineering strain ε = (60 − 50)/50 = 0.20. True strain εt = ln(60/50) = ln 1.2 = 0.182. Plastic deformation conserves volume, so A·L = A0·L0 and the current area is A0/1.2. True stress σt = F/A = σ(1 + ε) = 400 × 1.2 = 480 MPa. This is valid only while deformation is uniform, i.e. before necking starts.

questions.q: A beam of fixed length and square cross-section must have a specified bending stiffness at minimum mass. Which index should be maximised?
questions.why: Eliminating the side length using S ∝ EI/L³ with I ∝ b⁴ gives m ∝ ρ/E^(1/2), so E^(1/2)/ρ is maximised. E/ρ is the index for a tie loaded in tension, where stiffness is proportional to area rather than to b⁴. E^(1/3)/ρ is for a panel where only the thickness is free (I ∝ t³). σf^(2/3)/ρ is for a beam limited by strength rather than stiffness.

questions.q: Using approximate values E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2.7 Mg/m³ for aluminium and E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 Mg/m³ for steel, what is the mass of a stiffness-limited aluminium beam (square section, fixed length) as a fraction of the equivalent steel beam?
questions.why: Mass ∝ ρ/√E: aluminium 2.7/√70 = 0.323, steel 7.8/√210 = 0.538, ratio 0.60. 0.35 is just the density ratio 2.7/7.8, which ignores that aluminium needs a larger section to be as stiff. 1.04 uses the tie index ρ/E, the right ratio for a tension member but not for a beam. 0.50 uses ρ/E^(1/3), the panel index.

questions.q: Derive the material index for a light, stiff tie of given length L that must have axial stiffness S. Explain how you would use a log–log chart of E against ρ to pick candidates.
markScheme: Objective m = ALρ; constraint S = EA/L; free variable A
Eliminate A: m = SL²(ρ/E)
Minimise mass by maximising E/ρ
On log E vs log ρ, E/ρ = constant is a straight line of slope 1
Move the line towards high E, low ρ; materials above the line are better
questions.modelAnswer: Objective: minimise m = ALρ. Constraint: stiffness S = EA/L. The free variable is A, so A = SL/E and m = SL²(ρ/E). S and L are fixed by the design, so mass is minimised by maximising E/ρ. On a chart of log E against log ρ, E/ρ = M becomes log E = log ρ + log M, a line of slope 1. Every material on one line performs equally; sliding the line upwards and to the left until only a few materials remain above it identifies the best candidates, which are then screened for other requirements such as toughness and cost.

questions.q: A steel has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3. What is its shear modulus G?
questions.why: G = E/[2(1 + ν)] = 200/2.6 = 76.9 GPa. 153.8 GPa is E/(1 + ν), leaving out the factor of 2. 166.7 GPa is the bulk modulus E/[3(1 − 2ν)], the wrong relation. 100 GPa is E/2, which ignores Poisson's ratio altogether.

questions.q: Which type of bonding mainly governs the Young's modulus of a glassy thermoplastic such as PMMA at room temperature?
options: Secondary bonds (van der Waals and/or hydrogen) between chains
Covalent bonds along the polymer chains
questions.why: Elastic deformation of a glassy polymer is dominated by stretching the weak secondary bonds between chains, which is why its modulus is only a few GPa. The covalent bonds along the chains are strong but are not the main bonds being stretched when the bulk material deforms; picking them confuses chain strength with bulk stiffness. Metallic bonding requires delocalised electrons and is absent in polymers. Ionic bonding is found in ceramics and salts, not between neutral polymer chains.

questions.q: An aluminium alloy plate (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33) carries σx = 100 MPa and σy = 50 MPa with σz = 0. Calculate the three normal strains and the volumetric strain.
markScheme: ΔV/V = sum = 7.29 × 10⁻⁴ (check with (1 − 2ν)Σσ/E)

questions.q: A bond has stiffness S0 = 50 N/m and the equilibrium spacing is r0 = 0.2 nm. Estimate Young's modulus.
questions.why: E ≈ S0/r0 = 50/(0.2 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.5 × 10¹¹ Pa = 250 GPa. 0.25 GPa comes from converting 0.2 nm as if it were 0.2 µm (2 × 10⁻⁷ m). 25 GPa comes from taking r0 as 2 nm, a decimal-place slip. 2500 GPa comes from taking r0 as 0.02 nm (2 × 10⁻¹¹ m), a decimal-place slip in the other direction.

questions.q: Aligned carbon fibres (Ef = 230 GPa) in epoxy (Em = 3 GPa) at Vf = 0.6. What is the modulus perpendicular to the fibres according to the equal-stress model?
questions.why: 1/E⊥ = 0.6/230 + 0.4/3 = 0.00261 + 0.1333 = 0.1359, so E⊥ ≈ 7.4 GPa. 139 GPa is the equal-strain (Voigt) value, which applies along the fibres. 117 GPa is the plain average of 230 and 3, ignoring the volume fractions and the equal-stress model. 5.0 GPa comes from swapping the volume fractions in the equal-stress formula (0.4 for fibre, 0.6 for matrix).

questions.q: Using the idea of bond stiffness, explain why metals and ceramics have moduli of order 100 GPa while glassy polymers have moduli of a few GPa, and why an elastomer's modulus is lower still.
markScheme: E ≈ S0/r0, with r0 ≈ 0.2–0.3 nm for all
Metals and ceramics: primary bonds with S0 of roughly 10–200 N/m give E of tens to hundreds of GPa
Glassy polymers: deformation stretches secondary bonds between chains, S0 of roughly 0.5–2 N/m, giving E of a few GPa
Elastomers above Tg: secondary bonds melted; stiffness comes from entropy of cross-linked chains, E of a few MPa
questions.modelAnswer: Treating bonds as springs, stress ≈ force per bond divided by r0² and strain ≈ displacement/r0, so E ≈ S0/r0. Atomic spacings are similar (about 0.2–0.3 nm) in all solids, so differences in E come mainly from S0. Metals and ceramics are held by primary bonds with S0 of roughly 10–200 N/m, giving E of order 30–1000 GPa. In a glassy polymer the chains are covalently bonded, but bulk deformation mainly stretches the secondary bonds between chains, with S0 of roughly 0.5–2 N/m, so E is a few GPa. Above Tg these secondary bonds have melted; in a cross-linked elastomer the only resistance comes from the entropy of the chains being uncoiled, so E falls to a few MPa.

questions.q: A shear stress of 40 MPa acts on the slip plane of a dislocation with b = 0.25 nm. What is the force per unit length on the dislocation?
questions.why: f = τb = 40 × 10⁶ × 0.25 × 10⁻⁹ = 0.01 N/m. 1.6 × 10¹⁷ comes from dividing τ by b instead of multiplying. 1 × 10⁻⁵ N/m comes from reading 40 MPa as 40 kPa. 10 N/m comes from converting 0.25 nm as if it were 0.25 µm.

questions.q: For a pure screw dislocation, how is the Burgers vector oriented relative to the dislocation line?
questions.why: In a screw dislocation the lattice is sheared parallel to the dislocation line, so b is parallel to it. Perpendicular describes an edge dislocation, the other pure type. An intermediate angle such as 45° describes a mixed dislocation, not a pure screw. A zero Burgers vector would mean the circuit closes, i.e. a perfect crystal with no dislocation.

questions.q: Explain why the measured yield strength of a pure metal is far below the ideal strength of a perfect crystal, and why ceramics remain brittle even though they contain dislocations.
markScheme: Ideal strength requires all bonds across a plane to break simultaneously, giving roughly G/30 to G/2π
Dislocations allow slip by moving a line defect, breaking bonds one row at a time, at a much lower stress
Metals: low lattice resistance (non-directional metallic bonding) so dislocations glide easily
Ceramics: directional covalent/ionic bonds give high lattice resistance, so dislocations barely move and cracks propagate before yielding
questions.modelAnswer: In a perfect crystal, shearing one plane over another requires every bond across the plane to be stretched to its limit at the same time, giving an ideal shear strength of order G/30 to G/2π. Real crystals contain dislocations: moving one across the slip plane breaks and remakes bonds one row at a time, so slip occurs at a tiny fraction of the ideal stress. In metals the non-directional metallic bond gives low resistance to dislocation glide, so yield is low and ductility high. In ceramics the bonds are strongly directional (covalent) or involve charged ions, so the lattice resistance to dislocation motion is very high; at room temperature a crack grows from a flaw before dislocations can move, and the material fails in a brittle way.

questions.q: Precipitates in an aluminium alloy (G = 26 GPa, b = 0.286 nm) are 100 nm apart. Using the Orowan stress and σy ≈ 3τy, estimate the precipitation contribution to tensile yield strength.
questions.why: τ = Gb/L = 26 × 10⁹ × 0.286 × 10⁻⁹/100 × 10⁻⁹ = 74.4 MPa, and σy ≈ 3τ = 223 MPa. 74 MPa is the shear stress τ itself, without the factor of 3 for a polycrystal. 112 MPa comes from balancing τbL against only one line tension T instead of 2T, which halves τ to 37 MPa before multiplying by 3. 2230 MPa comes from taking b as 2.86 nm instead of 0.286 nm (misreading 2.86 Å as nanometres).

questions.q: According to the Hall–Petch relation, if the grain size of a metal is reduced by a factor of 4, the grain-boundary contribution k·d^(−1/2) to yield strength:
questions.why: The term goes as d^(−1/2); dividing d by 4 multiplies d^(−1/2) by √4 = 2. Quadrupling would follow if strength were proportional to 1/d, forgetting the square root. Halving would follow if the exponent were taken as +1/2 rather than −1/2. A factor of 16 would come from squaring the factor instead of taking its square root.

questions.q: Describe the heat treatment used to precipitation-harden an aerospace aluminium alloy and explain, in terms of dislocations, why the strength first rises and then falls with ageing time.
markScheme: Solution treatment at high temperature (around 500 °C) dissolves alloying elements in a single phase
Quench to room temperature traps them in a supersaturated solid solution
Ageing forms fine, closely spaced precipitates
Dislocations must bow between precipitates: τ ≈ Gb/L, so small spacing L gives high strength (peak aged)
Prolonged ageing coarsens precipitates, L increases, strength falls (over-aged)
questions.modelAnswer: The alloy is first solution treated at a high temperature (around 500 °C, depending on the alloy) so that the alloying elements dissolve in the aluminium. It is then quenched, trapping them in a supersaturated solid solution. Ageing at room temperature or a moderately raised temperature lets the excess solute come out as fine, closely spaced precipitates. A moving dislocation must bow out between the particles, and the stress needed is about τ ≈ Gb/L, where L is the spacing; so as fine precipitates form and L falls, strength rises to a peak. If ageing continues, larger precipitates grow at the expense of smaller ones, the spacing L increases and the strength falls: the alloy is over-aged.

questions.q: A fuselage section has hoop stress 60 MPa, axial stress 30 MPa and radial stress ≈ 0. What is the von Mises equivalent stress?
questions.why: σvm = √{½[(60 − 30)² + (30 − 0)² + (0 − 60)²]} = √{½(900 + 900 + 3600)} = √2700 = 52.0 MPa. 60 MPa is the Tresca equivalent σ1 − σ3. 30 MPa comes from applying Tresca to the two in-plane stresses only (60 − 30) and forgetting that the radial stress, zero, is the smallest principal stress. 90 MPa simply adds the hoop and axial stresses, which no yield criterion does.

questions.q: According to the von Mises criterion, a ductile metal in pure shear yields when τ equals:
questions.why: In pure shear σ1 = τ, σ2 = 0, σ3 = −τ, so ½[τ² + τ² + 4τ²] = 3τ² = σy², giving τ = σy/√3 ≈ 0.577σy. 0.5σy is the Tresca prediction. 0.707σy is 1/√2, from dividing by √2 instead of √3. 1.0σy assumes the material yields in shear at the same value as in tension, ignoring how shear stress relates to principal stresses.

questions.q: A thin-walled aluminium tube (σy = 275 MPa) carries an axial stress of 100 MPa and a torsional shear stress of 50 MPa. Find the principal stresses and the factor of safety against yield by Tresca and by von Mises.
markScheme: Principal stresses 50 ± √(50² + 50²) = 120.7 MPa and −20.7 MPa, third = 0
Tresca factor of safety 275/141.4 = 1.94
Von Mises: √(σ² + 3τ²) = 132.3 MPa
Von Mises factor of safety 275/132.3 = 2.08
questions.modelAnswer: Principal stresses: (100/2) ± √[(100/2)² + 50²] = 50 ± 70.7, so σ1 = 120.7 MPa and σ3 = −20.7 MPa, with σ2 = 0 (the radial stress). Tresca: σ1 − σ3 = 141.4 MPa (also √(100² + 4 × 50²)), giving a factor of safety of 275/141.4 = 1.94. Von Mises: √(σ² + 3τ²) = √(10,000 + 7,500) = 132.3 MPa, giving 275/132.3 = 2.08. Tresca is the more conservative of the two.

questions.q: A wide plate with Kc = 30 MPa√m carries a remote stress of 200 MPa. Taking Y = 1 for a central through-crack, what is the critical total crack length 2a?
questions.why: ac = (Kc/σ)²/π = (0.15)²/π = 7.16 × 10⁻³ m, so the total length 2a ≈ 14.3 mm. 7.2 mm is the half-length a, reported as if it were the full length. 45.0 mm comes from leaving out π (a = 0.0225 m, 2a = 45 mm). 95.5 mm comes from not squaring Kc/σ (a = 0.15/π m = 47.7 mm, doubled).

questions.q: If the working stress on a cracked component is doubled, what happens to the critical crack length for fast fracture?
options: It is unchanged, because Kc is a material property
questions.why: From Kc = Yσ√(πac), ac = (Kc/Yσ)²/π, so ac ∝ 1/σ² and doubling σ divides ac by 4. One half would follow if ac were proportional to 1/σ, forgetting the square. Kc is indeed a material constant, but the crack size that reaches it depends on stress, so ac does change. Doubling would require ac to increase with stress, the wrong direction.

questions.q: An aluminium alloy has Kc = 30 MPa√m, E = 70 GPa and σy = 300 MPa. Calculate its toughness Gc and the largest crack (half-length a, Y = 1) for which the material would yield before fast fracture. Comment on the result.
markScheme: Yield before fracture if a < Kc²/(πσy²)
Comment: cracks larger than about 3 mm would cause fast fracture before general yield; inspection must find smaller cracks or stresses must be lower
questions.modelAnswer: Gc = Kc²/E = (30 × 10⁶)²/(70 × 10⁹) = 1.29 × 10⁴ J/m² ≈ 12.9 kJ/m². Setting the fracture stress equal to the yield stress: Kc = σy√(πa), so a = (Kc/σy)²/π = (0.1)²/π = 3.2 × 10⁻³ m = 3.2 mm. Cracks with a half-length below about 3 mm let the material yield (and so give visible warning) before fast fracture; longer cracks would cause brittle-type fast fracture below the yield stress. So inspection must be able to find cracks smaller than this, or working stresses must be kept well below yield.

questions.q: A ceramic has Weibull modulus m = 10 and reference stress σ0 = 300 MPa (for the test volume). What is the probability that a sample of the same volume survives a stress of 200 MPa?
questions.why: Ps = exp[−(200/300)^10] = exp(−0.0173) = 0.983. 0.017 is the failure probability, 1 − Ps. 0.513 comes from using m = 1, i.e. exp(−2/3), forgetting the exponent. 0.667 is just the stress ratio σ/σ0, not a probability from the Weibull expression.

questions.q: Which of these materials is most likely to show significant creep at room temperature under a steady load?
questions.why: Creep becomes significant when the temperature is a sizeable fraction of the melting point or near Tg; polyethylene's Tg is far below room temperature, so at 20 °C it creeps readily. Alumina has a melting point above 2000 °C, so room temperature is a tiny fraction of it. Nickel superalloys are designed to resist creep at turbine temperatures, so room temperature poses no creep problem. Titanium alloys melt around 1600 °C and do not creep significantly at room temperature under normal design stresses.

questions.q: A batch of ceramic test bars has m = 10 and σ0 = 300 MPa. (a) What fraction of bars fails at 200 MPa? (b) A component has ten times the volume of a test bar. What is its survival probability at 200 MPa? (c) Explain the result and what it means for design.
markScheme: (a) Ps = exp[−(2/3)^10] = 0.983, so about 1.7% fail
(c) Larger volume contains more flaws, so a critical flaw is more likely
(c) Design must use a lower stress for large components, or improve m (better processing, proof testing)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Ps = exp[−(200/300)^10] = exp(−0.0173) = 0.983, so about 1.7% of bars fail. (b) For ten times the volume, Ps = exp[−10 × 0.0173] = exp(−0.173) = 0.84, so about 16% of components would fail. (c) Brittle strength is set by the largest flaw, and a larger volume is more likely to contain a large one, so strength falls with size. Designers must use a lower allowable stress for large ceramic parts, improve processing to raise m and reduce flaw size, or proof-test components to remove weak ones.

questions.q:
A pressurised fuselage is modelled as a thin-walled cylinder of radius 2.0 m and skin thickness 2.0 mm, made of an aluminium alloy with σy = 300 MPa, Kc = 30 MPa√m and E = 70 GPa. The cabin pressure differential is 60 kPa.
(a) Calculate the hoop and axial stresses in the skin. [3]
(b) Find the factor of safety against yielding using the Tresca and the von Mises criteria. [5]
(c) A through-thickness crack runs along the length of the fuselage (so it is opened by the hoop stress). Taking Y = 1, find the critical crack length 2a. [4]
(d) Calculate the toughness Gc and the half-length below which the alloy would yield before fast fracture. [4]
(e) Discuss what these results imply for inspection and design of the fuselage. [4]
markScheme: (b) Tresca: σ1 − σ3 = 60 MPa, FoS = 5.0
(b) Von Mises: √{½[30² + 30² + 60²]} = 52.0 MPa, FoS = 5.77
(d) Gc = Kc²/E ≈ 12.9 kJ/m²; a = (Kc/σy)²/π ≈ 3.2 mm

(e) Uniform stresses are far below yield and the critical crack is long, but stress concentrations at windows and joints, fatigue crack growth from pressurisation cycles and multiple-site damage reduce margins
(e) Damage-tolerant design: inspection intervals so cracks are found well below ac; crack stoppers, tough alloys; reference to Comet failures
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Hoop stress σθ = pr/t = (60 × 10³ × 2.0)/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 60 MPa. Axial stress σz = pr/2t = 30 MPa. The radial stress is at most the 0.06 MPa pressure on the inner surface, negligible: σr ≈ 0.

(b) Principal stresses: σ1 = 60, σ2 = 30, σ3 = 0 MPa. Tresca: σ1 − σ3 = 60 MPa, so the factor of safety = 300/60 = 5.0. Von Mises: σvm = √{½[(60 − 30)² + (30 − 0)² + (0 − 60)²]} = √{½(900 + 900 + 3600)} = √2700 = 52.0 MPa, so the factor of safety = 300/52.0 = 5.77. The skin is far from general yield.

(c) A longitudinal crack is opened by the hoop stress. Fast fracture when Kc = σθ√(πa): a = (Kc/σθ)²/π = (30/60)²/π = 0.25/π = 0.0796 m. The critical total length is 2a ≈ 0.159 m, about 159 mm.

(d) Gc = Kc²/E = (30 × 10⁶)²/(70 × 10⁹) ≈ 1.29 × 10⁴ J/m² = 12.9 kJ/m². Yield before fracture requires σy√(πa) < Kc, i.e. a < (Kc/σy)²/π = (0.1)²/π = 3.2 × 10⁻³ m. So in a region stressed to yield (e.g. at a stress concentration) a crack of half-length above about 3 mm would cause fast fracture before the material yields.

(e) Under the nominal pressurisation stress the skin has a large margin against yield, and a crack would have to be about 16 cm long before fast fracture. However, the stresses near windows, doors and fastener holes are several times the nominal value (a circular hole alone gives a factor of 3), and every flight is a pressurisation cycle, so fatigue cracks can start there and grow. Near such features the critical crack is much shorter. Hence the structure is designed to be damage tolerant: inspection intervals are set so that cracks are found well before they reach critical length; crack-stopper straps and frames limit crack growth; tough, fatigue-resistant alloys are chosen; and cut-out corners are generously radiused. The 1954 Comet losses, caused by fatigue cracks from corners of fuselage openings, are the classic example of what happens when these effects are underestimated.

questions.q:
A designer must choose a material for a light, stiff wing rib member, modelled as a beam of fixed length L with a square cross-section of side b that may be varied. It must have a specified bending stiffness S = C·EI/L³ (C is a constant).
(a) Derive the material index to be maximised for minimum mass. [6]
(b) Using the approximate data below, rank the materials and find the mass of each beam relative to the steel one. Steel: E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7.8 Mg/m³; aluminium alloy: 70 GPa, 2.7 Mg/m³; titanium alloy: 115 GPa, 4.5 Mg/m³; CFRP (laminate): 100 GPa, 1.6 Mg/m³; spruce (along grain): 10 GPa, 0.45 Mg/m³. [6]
(c) Explain how this selection would be carried out on a log E–log ρ chart. [3]
(d) Spruce ranks highly. Discuss why it is not used for modern airliner structures, and what other factors decide the final choice. [5]
markScheme: (a) Objective m = b²Lρ; constraint S = CEb⁴/(12L³); free variable b
(b) Indices (GPa^½ per Mg/m³): spruce 7.0, CFRP 6.3, Al 3.1, Ti 2.4, steel 1.9
(b) Relative mass ρ/√E vs steel: spruce 0.26, CFRP 0.30, Al 0.60, Ti 0.78, steel 1
(c) Index lines of slope 2 on log E vs log ρ; move the line up/left; materials above it are better
(d) Wood: variability, moisture sensitivity, decay, anisotropy, low absolute strength/stiffness so sections become bulky, joining and certification issues
(d) Final choice also needs strength, toughness/damage tolerance, fatigue, environment, manufacturing, cost and certification
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Objective: minimise mass m = b²Lρ. Constraint: S = CEI/L³ with I = b⁴/12, so S = CEb⁴/(12L³). Free variable: b. Rearranging, b⁴ = 12SL³/(CE), so b² = (12SL³/CE)^(1/2). Substituting, m = (12S/C)^(1/2)·L^(5/2)·(ρ/E^(1/2)). S, C and L are fixed by the design, so the mass is minimised by maximising M = E^(1/2)/ρ.

(b) Values of √E/ρ: steel √210/7.8 = 14.5/7.8 = 1.86; aluminium √70/2.7 = 8.37/2.7 = 3.10; titanium √115/4.5 = 10.7/4.5 = 2.38; CFRP √100/1.6 = 10/1.6 = 6.25; spruce √10/0.45 = 3.16/0.45 = 7.03. Ranking: spruce > CFRP > aluminium > titanium > steel. Since mass ∝ ρ/√E, the relative masses are: steel 1.00, titanium 0.78, aluminium 0.60, CFRP 0.30, spruce 0.26. A stiffness-limited beam in CFRP weighs under a third of a steel one.

(c) On a chart of log E against log ρ, the condition E^(1/2)/ρ = M becomes log E = 2 log ρ + 2 log M, a family of parallel lines of slope 2. Draw one, then slide it towards the top left (higher E, lower ρ) until only a small set of materials lies above it; these are the best candidates, all of which perform at least as well as any material on the line.

(d) Wood scores well because it is very light, and the index favours low density when E enters with a low power. But its absolute stiffness and strength are low, so sections become thick; it is strongly anisotropic, its properties vary from piece to piece and with moisture content, it can decay, and it is difficult to join and certify to modern standards. The final choice must also consider strength and the strength index, toughness and damage tolerance, fatigue behaviour, temperature range, corrosion and environmental resistance, manufacturing route and cost, repairability and certification. This is why airliners use aluminium alloys and, increasingly, CFRP, even though wood had a historical role in aircraft such as the de Havilland Mosquito.
